title: Jeremiah 48:1–17
context: The LORD of Armies pronounces a long oracle against Moab, Israel’s neighbor east of the Dead Sea. Town after town is named as the destroyer comes: Nebo, Kiriathaim, Heshbon, Horonaim, and others, most of whose locations are identified only tentatively. Moab’s trust in its works, its treasures, and its god Chemosh will fail. The LORD calls the destroyer to do its work fully and pictures Moab as wine that has never been poured from vessel to vessel. Much of the oracle’s wording is shared with Isaiah 15-16, which can be read alongside it without merging the two. Both traditions read the chapter as the LORD’s just rule over the nations, not only over Israel.

verses.text: Of Moab. The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: “Woe to Nebo! For it is laid waste. Kiriathaim is disappointed. It is taken. Misgab is put to shame and broken down.
verses.arminianNotes: Of Moab. Arminian readers note that the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, speaks over a foreign nation, showing that his justice reaches beyond the covenant people to every kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the oracle opens with a cry of woe over Nebo and Kiriathaim. The sites are usually placed in the Moabite highlands, though identifications are tentative; Ezekiel 25:9 also names Kiriathaim.

verses.text: The praise of Moab is no more. In Heshbon they have devised evil against her: ‘Come! Let’s cut her off from being a nation.’ You also, Madmen, will be brought to silence. The sword will pursue you.
verses.arminianNotes: The praise of Moab is no more. Arminian readers see the end of Moab’s renown, as plans are devised against her in Heshbon to cut her off from being a nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the wordplay many find between Heshbon and devised, and between Madmen and silence, though such sound plays are hard to carry into English. The site of Madmen is uncertain.

verses.text: The sound of a cry from Horonaim, desolation and great destruction!
verses.arminianNotes: The sound of a cry from Horonaim, desolation and great destruction! Arminian readers hear the oracle moving from place to place, so that the reader senses judgment spreading through the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Horonaim also appears in Isaiah 15:5. Its location is debated, though it is often placed in the south of Moab, near the descent toward the Dead Sea.

verses.text: Moab is destroyed. Her little ones have caused a cry to be heard.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab is destroyed. Arminian readers note that the cry of little ones is heard, a sober reminder that judgment on a nation brings suffering to its most vulnerable people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the text records the cry without lingering on it. Both traditions read the line with grief rather than satisfaction, as the oracle itself does in later verses.

verses.text: For they will go up by the ascent of Luhith with continual weeping. For at the descent of Horonaim they have heard the distress of the cry of destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: For they will go up by the ascent of Luhith with continual weeping. Arminian readers note the close resemblance to Isaiah 15:5, which also mentions the ascent of Luhith and the way to Horonaim.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the two passages share wording without being identical, and they can be read side by side. The ascent of Luhith is not securely identified.

verses.text: Flee! Save your lives! Be like the juniper bush in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes: Flee! Save your lives! Arminian readers hear an urgent command to escape, the language of a land overrun where survival itself becomes the only aim of its people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the comparison to the juniper bush in the wilderness. The plant is not certainly identified, but the image seems to picture a lonely, stunted life in barren country.

verses.text: For, because you have trusted in your works and in your treasures, you also will be taken. Chemosh will go out into captivity, his priests and his princes together.
verses.arminianNotes: For, because you have trusted in your works and in your treasures, you also will be taken. Arminian readers see misplaced trust exposed: what Moab relied on cannot save it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Chemosh, the god of Moab named in 1 Kings 11:7 and 11:33, goes into captivity with his priests and princes. The god cannot protect his worshipers or even himself.

verses.text: The destroyer will come on every city, and no city will escape; the valley also will perish, and the plain will be destroyed, as the LORD has spoken.
verses.arminianNotes: The destroyer will come on every city, and no city will escape; Arminian readers see the thoroughness of the judgment that the LORD has spoken, reaching valley and plain alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the closing phrase, as the LORD has spoken. The destroyer is not named here, and the oracle leaves the agent general while stressing the certainty of the word.

verses.text: Give wings to Moab, that she may fly and get herself away: and her cities will become a desolation, without anyone to dwell in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Give wings to Moab, that she may fly and get herself away: Arminian readers hear a bitter wish that Moab could escape, since its cities will be left without anyone to dwell in them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the opening words are difficult, and translations differ on the sense of the image. The point appears to be that flight is the only hope left, and even that is uncertain.

verses.text: “Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD negligently; and cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood.
verses.arminianNotes: Cursed is he who does the work of the LORD negligently; Arminian readers read the line in its setting as a charge to the agents of this particular judgment on Moab, not as a general saying about diligence in work.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the second half, cursed is he who keeps back his sword from blood, ties the verse to this commissioned judgment. Neither tradition treats it as a license for violence by believers today.

verses.text: “Moab has been at ease from his youth, and he has settled on his dregs, and has not been emptied from vessel to vessel, neither has he gone into captivity; therefore his taste remains in him, and his scent is not changed.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab has been at ease from his youth, and he has settled on his dregs, Arminian readers see complacency pictured as wine left undisturbed, a people who never faced upheaval and so never changed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the image of wine not emptied from vessel to vessel, so its taste remains. Zephaniah 1:12 uses similar language of those settled on their dregs in Jerusalem.

verses.text: Therefore behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will send to him those who pour off, and they will pour him off; and they will empty his vessels, and break their containers in pieces.
verses.arminianNotes: Therefore behold, the days come, Arminian readers see the wine image continued: those who pour off will come, emptying Moab’s vessels and breaking its containers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD himself sends those who pour off. The image moves from settled ease to violent disturbance, a reversal of the complacency described in the previous verse.

verses.text: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence. Arminian readers see a warning that false trust brings shame, for Israel and Moab alike.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Bethel was a site of Jeroboam’s golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29). The comparison sets Moab’s idolatry beside Israel’s own, without excusing either.

verses.text: “How do you say, ‘We are mighty men, and valiant men for the war’?
verses.arminianNotes: How do you say, ‘We are mighty men, and valiant men for the war’? Arminian readers hear the LORD challenging Moab’s boast of military strength, which will prove empty in the day of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the question exposes self-confidence. Human strength is not condemned in itself, but trust in it apart from God is shown to be folly.

verses.text: Moab is laid waste, and they have gone up into his cities, and his chosen young men have gone down to the slaughter,” says the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: Moab is laid waste, and they have gone up into his cities, Arminian readers see the boasting answered by the fall of Moab’s chosen young men, gone down to the slaughter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the title the King, whose name is the LORD of Armies. The one who speaks is the true king, in contrast to the claimed might of Moab’s warriors.

verses.text: “The calamity of Moab is near to come, and his affliction hurries fast.
verses.arminianNotes: The calamity of Moab is near to come, and his affliction hurries fast. Arminian readers hear urgency, as the oracle stresses that the judgment is not distant but close at hand.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the nearness of calamity underlines the certainty of the word. The prophets often speak of coming judgment as already near, whatever the exact timing.

verses.text: All you who are around him, bemoan him; and all you who know his name, say, ‘How the strong staff is broken, the beautiful rod!’
verses.arminianNotes: All you who are around him, bemoan him; Arminian readers note that the neighbors are called to lament, not to gloat. Their words, How the strong staff is broken, the beautiful rod! are a dirge over fallen power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the staff and rod picture Moab’s power and rule. The call to mourn sets the tone for later laments in the chapter, where grief accompanies judgment.
